commonErrors.example: A learner writes on the worksheet that a centrifugal force really does fling passengers outward in a turn.

fixIt.corrected: No outward fling exists: your body wants to keep going straight while the seat pushes you inward - the inward push is the real force. The sensation is inertia, not an outward force.
fixIt.prompt: Fix it: state what actually pushes a passenger in a sharp turn, naming the direction of the real force.

commonErrors.misconception: A centrifugal force flings you outward in a sharp turn.

commonErrors.example: On the exit ticket, a learner picks the statement that a centrifugal force pushing outward is the force that acts on the passenger in a sharp turn.

fixIt.corrected: An inward, centre-seeking push from the seat and door; there is no outward force.
fixIt.prompt: Fix it: explain in one sentence why there is no outward force on a passenger in a sharp turn.

commonErrors.misconception: A centrifugal force flings you outward in a sharp turn.

modelAnswers.answer: The force quadruples (factor of 4). F = mv^2/r, so doubling v multiplies v^2 by 4 while m and r stay fixed.
modelAnswers.question: A satellite in a circular orbit doubles its speed while staying at the same orbital radius. By what factor does the required centripetal force change? Explain using F = mv^2/r.

modelAnswers.answer: F = mv^2/r = 1200 x 225 / 50 = 5400 N, directed toward the centre of the bend (supplied by friction).
modelAnswers.question: A car of mass 1200 kg rounds a bend of radius 50 m at 15 m/s. Calculate the centripetal force needed and state its direction.

nextSteps: Reteach the fling-off trap from the paired notes trap before any further mechanics work: the only horizontal force on a turning passenger is the inward push from the seat and door.
Practise stating the direction to the centre in the working whenever a centripetal force is calculated.
strengths: Most of the class can compute the centripetal force, such as 15 N, from F = mv^2/r = 0.50 x 36 / 1.2 on the worksheet.
The class can state the period of a geostationary orbit as 24 hours, matching the Earth's rotation on the exit ticket.
